sources.text: Climbing, indoor bouldering. Youth recreational group, not a performance squad. I do a friendly local competition sometimes, but I am not chasing a ranking.
sources.question: What sport are we focusing on right now?

sources.text: I want to finish the blue overhang problem I have been working on because solving it would feel good. I like hard problems. I do not want climbing to become a job.
sources.question: What would you love to achieve in your sport, and why does it matter to you?

sources.text: I can work out foot placements and change a method when the first one fails. Last Tuesday a different starting foot let me get one move farther on the blue problem.
sources.question: What feels strongest about the way you are performing right now?

sources.text: I can spend the whole session trying to explain one move and run out of time to try the next idea. On Thursday I watched and talked about the middle section, then had only one go left.
sources.question: What part of your performance would you most like to improve?

sources.text: By November 2 I would like to finish that problem, or be able to explain what I tried and which approach gets me farther. I would be disappointed not to finish, but learning something real still counts.
sources.question: What would make the next six to eight weeks feel successful in your sport?

sources.text: Tuesday and Thursday at the climbing gym, 90 minutes each. Saturday sometimes a walk with a friend. No extra finger training. My week is okay and I want to keep unplanned time.
sources.question: What does a normal training week look like for you?

sources.text: I want each session to answer one useful question about the climb. I do not want to collect exercises without knowing what they are for.
sources.question: What do you most want your training to help you do better?

sources.text: Writing the part I could not solve and trying another method next time helped on a previous route. Tuesday I changed the starting foot and got farther on this one.
sources.question: Which part of your training seems to be helping most?

sources.text: Several people call different suggestions while I am looking. I ask why and we can spend ages discussing. Last Thursday I ran out of time. Coach would like me to try first more often; I want to understand enough to choose.
sources.question: Which part feels confusing, hard to keep up with, or not useful?

sources.text: One clear question to explore, one person giving advice at a time, and enough of the same session left to actually climb. I do not want another session or a training spreadsheet.
sources.question: What would make your training week work better for you?

sources.text: I can be curious, try something that may fail, then change it. I am not thinking about explaining myself to everyone at once.
sources.question: When you are playing with confidence, what is different about you?

sources.text: I get exact and quiet when several people ask why I am stuck. On Thursday I stopped answering for a bit. I was frustrated with the problem, not necessarily angry with them.
sources.question: When the pressure goes up, what usually happens for you?

sources.text: Quiet and a clear account of the part that failed. A short pause away from the conversation can help. Sometimes I just want to go home, and I do not know a perfect reset.
sources.question: After a mistake or a bad performance, what helps you get back into it?

sources.text: Try a reasonable idea before I have the perfect explanation. I still want to know what we are testing. I do not want brave to mean ignoring the instructor.
sources.question: What would you most like to handle better mentally in your sport?

sources.text: Ask one question and give me time. State what result you mean. If people disagree about a method, I would rather compare ideas than pretend we all agree.
sources.question: What do you need from the people around you to compete at your best?

sources.text: Year 12. I like engineering and physics. I changed one subject after checking the course outline. School is mostly going okay.
sources.question: How is school going for you right now?

sources.text: I am good at diagrams and building a test. I can spend too long comparing options in the design project. We nearly missed a parts order before. For the current project, the design choice is due September 25.
sources.question: Which parts of school feel strongest, and which need help?

sources.text: Choose a workable design and submit it by September 25, then test and improve it. It does not have to be the best possible design in the world.
sources.question: What would you like to achieve in school this term?

sources.text: Possibly engineering or repair work. I want to be good at something useful. I am comparing college and apprenticeship routes; I have not chosen one.
sources.question: Where would you like school to lead for you?

sources.text: The two climbing sessions fit. I have a Friday project block for the design choice, and I want to keep it. I do not need MORE to fill every free hour.
sources.question: How are school and sport fitting together in your week?

bos_sources.headline: Clear enough to change course
bos_sources.text:
One of the clearest things about you is that order and flexibility belong together. You like knowing what the job is, what finished means, and what can be checked. Once that frame is solid, you are quite willing to replace a failed method, change your mind after a test, or stop repeating something that teaches you nothing. The plan gives you something steady enough to experiment against; it is not a promise to defend the first idea.

What draws you in is not difficulty for its own sake. A problem becomes interesting when you can understand it, affect the outcome, and learn something real from it. Repairing an old speaker mattered because you wanted to know why it had stopped working. More broadly, you seem to care about becoming good at something useful. At the same time, you do not want every interest turned into a job or public achievement. Making things can matter without taking over your whole identity.

That same balance appears in groups. You will speak when you think you can move the work forward, perhaps by naming a test, finding useful information, or breaking a large problem into smaller parts. You are also comfortable with someone else presenting, and you do not need to control every role. This suggests that useful influence often matters more to you than visibility. You are not purely a solo problem-solver either: once the question is clear, you will use manuals, examples, knowledgeable people, and divided work.

With people, you are selective rather than simply distant. A trusted friend and a shared interest can hold your attention for ages, while a group with several conversations at once can wear you out. After connection, you often need space. That space does not cancel the connection; it seems to protect your ability to return as yourself. Your friends also know a more playful version of you—the one who makes terrible jokes and definitely does not speak like a manual all the time.

One of the harder parts is that your care may exist before it becomes visible. You often start with the missing information, the exact point of disagreement, or the result that is needed. To you, that can be a serious and fair way to handle the problem. Someone else may first hear a sharp question or a solution and miss the concern underneath. You already notice this gap: you know you can solve before showing that you listened, and you sometimes wonder whether a person felt heard. The issue is not a lack of care; it is often the order in which care and problem-solving become visible.

Your pace changes with the situation. With a practical unknown, you often read enough to begin and then learn through action. With an important choice, you are more likely to compare what each option will really involve and whether it will still fit later. Unfamiliar social situations are less inviting, especially when expectations are unstated. Under several questions or demands for an instant answer, you become more exact and less talkative. Short answers or leaving can protect thinking space, but if you do not name that need, another person may read the pause as anger or rejection.

So you have both a quick experimental side and a slower, protective side. The first likes a clear problem, an early attempt, and honest feedback from the result. The second appears when the choice has longer consequences, the social meaning is unclear, or too many things arrive at once. Across both sides, you are protecting much the same things: accuracy, a reason you can respect, room to make your own judgment, and relationships where clear words and real trust matter. You are practical without being only serious, organized without being fixed, and connected without needing constant company.

bos_sources.headline: Useful without becoming a performance
bos_sources.text:
You do not describe yourself mainly through a title, a team role, or a future job. The things that matter to you—making things, time to yourself, and a few people you trust—suggest a life that feels worthwhile from the inside. Engineering or repair work may become part of that life, but you are keeping it as a possibility rather than turning it into a fixed plan.

Being good at something useful matters to you. That seems less about collecting attention and more about having skill that does something real. Your group choices fit that idea: you may offer a direction or useful test, then let somebody else present. Recognition may still matter sometimes, but you do not seem to need every contribution to become a performance.

You also protect the right for an interest to stay an interest. Saying that a hobby does not have to become your job leaves room for enjoyment, curiosity, and choice. It means your future does not have to swallow everything you like now. Trusted relationships and private time sit beside competence, not below it.

A flat label would miss you. You can like people and need space, enjoy a plan and change the method, keep going for a reason and stop when the reason disappears. You also make terrible jokes with friends. Your precise working voice is real, but it is not the whole person. You seem most yourself when usefulness, independence, closeness, and playfulness are all allowed to exist without one taking over.
bos_sources.takeaway: You want skill to be useful without letting achievement become your whole identity.

bos_sources.headline: Make it clear, then test it
bos_sources.text:
Your mind seems to work best when the problem can be made stable enough to inspect. You look for a diagram, manual, example, outline, or written note; gather enough to start; then let the result tell you what to change. You do not need every detail before the first attempt. What matters is having a clear enough picture to make the attempt informative.

Other people fit into this process as useful sources, not as substitutes for your judgment. You asked a teacher about a possible subject and asked someone knowledgeable about a repair after making the question clear. A photograph, written comment, or specific explanation gives you something you can revisit instead of having to guess what was meant.

When the choice matters beyond today, you slow the process down. In changing a school subject, you checked what each option would actually involve and asked whether it would still interest you a year later. That is practical future-thinking: you do not only imagine an outcome; you inspect the route that would lead there.

Your precision has a tradeoff. Sometimes the search for the exact explanation or best option can continue after the situation only needs a workable choice. When an order deadline became visible, you were able to choose, so exactness does not trap you completely. Your experimenting is clearest with problems that give usable feedback; crowded or unfamiliar social situations do not offer the same clean signals.
bos_sources.takeaway: You build a clear enough picture to try, then let results change your next move.

bos_sources.headline: Let the human message show
bos_sources.text:
Clear communication, for you, usually means naming the thing itself. You can use feedback that says what is wrong and what the finished result needs to be. Written comments help because they stay still long enough to check. Hints that assume you already know what someone means are much harder when you genuinely do not know which part they expect you to supply.

The main misunderstanding is often between what you mean to do and what becomes visible. Asking for missing information may feel like the most honest route to understanding, yet you have been told it can sound rude. Care, patience, or reassurance may remain inside the message while the question itself lands first. Tone, timing, and the other person’s expectations also matter, but this explains why two people can leave the same exchange with different impressions.

In disagreement, you tend to define the exact difference and look for a fair way to compare the options. When a robotics teammate felt dismissed, you asked them to explain and suggested testing both ideas. That move treated both designs seriously, yet you were still unsure whether the person felt fully heard. For you, listening and testing may belong together; for someone else, the listening may need to become visible before the test.

When you are under strain, your communication gets narrower: fewer words, more exactness, and sometimes leaving the conversation. If you know you need time but do not say it, the pause can carry a meaning you never intended. A brief sign that you heard the person, or that you need time rather than agreement, may help your actual purpose survive the moment.
bos_sources.takeaway: Your clearest words work best when your care and need for time are clear too.

bos_sources.headline: Depth, trust, and room afterward
bos_sources.text:
Your social life seems to depend more on the quality of attention than on simply being with or without people. You can talk for ages with someone you trust about a shared interest. A group becomes costly when several conversations compete at once, and afterward you often need space. That is selective depth, not a lack of interest in connection. Closeness and solitude are both real needs for you.

Trust appears to grow around clarity. You feel respected when people use clear words and take your answer seriously. You try to return that respect by not pretending to agree. Smoothness for its own sake matters less than knowing that both people are being real, even if the answer is inconvenient.

There is a tension here. You may show respect by taking an idea seriously enough to question it, solve it, or compare it fairly. Another person may experience respect first through being listened to without an immediate solution. Neither need cancel the other, but the order can affect whether your honesty feels connecting or distancing.

Unfamiliar social events interest you less than unfamiliar practical problems. The reason is not completely clear: noise, divided attention, unclear expectations, lack of a shared topic, or unfamiliar people could each matter. Familiarity changes your range. With friends, humor and long conversations appear; after the interaction, quiet helps you recover the room to be yourself again.
bos_sources.takeaway: You connect deeply through trust and shared focus, then need space to recover your attention.

bos_sources.headline: A reason keeps effort attached
bos_sources.text:
Effort comes more easily when you can see why the task matters. A problem you can work out offers curiosity, control over the next move, and a real result. By contrast, instructions that change without any explanation weaken the logic of the task. It is not change itself that bothers you; it is being asked to follow a moving rule without understanding its purpose.

Once a reason is present, your persistence is flexible. You can stay with the problem while refusing to stay loyal to a method that repeatedly fails. A different connection, a new angle, or another source of information can keep the work alive. This is not constant novelty-seeking. You usually keep the goal or test steady while changing the route.

You are also willing to stop. You left an online course because it was mostly covering things you already knew, so continuing would not have offered much learning. That does not mean every boring task loses your effort. Necessary work can still be repetitive, and it is not yet clear which reasons—responsibility, deadline, usefulness to someone else, or a larger goal—keep you attached then.

Your standards can both power and slow your effort. Wanting the exact explanation can produce a better question and fewer guesses. It can also keep comparison going after the practical need has shifted to good enough for now. You can make that shift when the time cost is clear. The useful distinction for you seems to be whether more checking will change the outcome or only delay it.
bos_sources.takeaway: A reason keeps you engaged; it does not require you to keep using a failing route.

bos_sources.headline: Too much at once makes you quieter
bos_sources.text:
Ordinarily, one clear problem and time to think leave you able to work through what is happening. Pressure changes you most when demands stack up: several questions, noise, or an expectation of an instant answer. The number of things to track seems more important than difficulty alone. A hard problem can still be manageable when it stays one problem.

In those busier moments, you become more exact and less talkative. Answers shorten, the conversation becomes harder to follow, and leaving may become the cleanest way to reduce input. That pause may be sensible, not a failure. The complication is that you do not always explain your need for time before you go.

Without that explanation, another person may fill in the blank. A friend once thought you were angry with them when your frustration was with the project. That does not mean every quiet moment will be misread. It shows how pressure can hide the difference between what you feel, what you are trying to protect, and what someone else can see.

After not finishing a climbing route, you wrote down the unsolved part and later tried another approach. At other times, you simply want to go home. Quiet walking or working alone on something small may give your attention room to settle, but you are still figuring out how reliably that helps you re-enter. Your current week is okay, so this describes a change under strain rather than your state all the time.
bos_sources.takeaway: Too many inputs narrow your words; one clear problem and time make more of you available.

bos_sources.headline: Turning unknowns into workable parts
bos_sources.text:
One distinctive strength is your way of turning a large unknown into a set of smaller, answerable questions. Instead of treating the whole problem as one block, you look for tests, missing information, and parts that can be handled separately. This gives uncertainty a shape. It can also give a group a practical next move when discussion is circling.

You pair that with resourcefulness. You will investigate on your own, but you also use manuals, diagrams, examples, photographs, teachers, knowledgeable people, and shared roles. Asking who wants which part is not giving the problem away; it recognizes that doing everything yourself wastes time. Your independence includes knowing when another source can improve the result.

Another strength is structured adaptability. You can keep a purpose, test, or definition of finished steady while changing the route after a result proves the first method wrong. That allows you to be organized without being stuck. You do not change merely because something is new; you change when there is a reason you can inspect.

These strengths have honest tradeoffs. Breaking things down can become prolonged comparison when only a workable choice is needed. Moving quickly toward a fair test can make another person’s need to be heard less visible. Selective direction can also leave the final ownership unclear if everyone is waiting. None of these erase the strength. They show where your useful, exact approach may need a clearer time line, role, or human signal. You have mainly described this in technical groups; at home or elsewhere, you may contribute differently.
bos_sources.takeaway: You make uncertainty workable by turning it into tests, resources, and shared parts.

bos_sources.headline: Clarity with room to choose
bos_sources.text:
You seem to have your widest range when clarity and choice work together. A meaningful reason, a visible endpoint, and information you can inspect reduce the energy spent guessing. Freedom to revise the method keeps that clarity from becoming a cage. This combination can fit schoolwork, making and repair, group projects, and sport problems, although the exact balance may differ in each place.

Your surroundings matter too. One question at a time and enough response time help you keep hold of what you want to say. Written feedback, a diagram, or a clear example can make school and practical tasks easier to enter. When advice or roles are vague, you may spend more effort decoding the request than doing the work itself.

With people, thriving does not mean constant company. You want a few trusted relationships, shared interests, and clear words, while also needing quiet afterward. Time alone is not the opposite of belonging for you; it helps preserve it. Unplanned time matters for a similar reason. Even though you like plans, not every part of the day needs to be assigned before you reach it.

After a difficult moment, you may turn toward less input, a quiet walk, or one small task before taking on more. The larger fit is not a perfect routine. It is a life with enough purpose to engage you, enough structure to orient you, enough freedom to change course, and enough space for trust, humor, and your own attention.
bos_sources.takeaway: You thrive with clear purpose, adjustable methods, trusted people, and protected room that remains your own.

bos_sources.headline: Your command pattern
bos_sources.text: You step in when a direction can move the work forward, but you do not need every decision, role, or visible moment. You prefer shared ownership over taking charge of the whole group. Clear roles let you propose a test, make your own choice, or divide work without owning everything. If no one owns the final decision, the last step may stay unclear; reactions also need room. This is clearest in a school choice and technical groups, not every setting.
bos_sources.takeaway: You step in when a direction can move the work forward, but you do not need every decision, role, or visible moment. You prefer shared ownership over taking charge of the whole group.

bos_sources.headline: Your tempo pattern
bos_sources.text: You often read enough to begin and learn by trying. With an important choice, several questions, or social pressure, you prefer more room before speaking or deciding. Brief preparation, action, and feedback suit practical problems; one question at a time protects your response when things get busy. Instant answers and rapid switching may make you quieter, so others may miss that you are still thinking. Your pace changes with the stakes and number of demands; this is a preference, not an ability grade.
bos_sources.takeaway: You often read enough to begin and learn by trying. With an important choice, several questions, or social pressure, you prefer more room before speaking or deciding.

bos_sources.headline: Your relational awareness pattern
bos_sources.text: You begin with clear words and the exact issue more than unspoken social hints. You do check impact, especially when someone names it, but care may become visible after the solution. Direct feedback gives you something usable, and asking what the disagreement is can reopen an honest conversation. Solutions, short answers, or leaving may hide care and listening that you feel but have not shown. This describes where your attention starts, not how much you care or whether another person’s reading is correct.
bos_sources.takeaway: You begin with clear words and the exact issue more than unspoken social hints. You do check impact, especially when someone names it, but care may become visible after the solution.

bos_sources.headline: Your precision pattern
bos_sources.text: You naturally seek exact information, checkable details, and a clear result. You can accept a workable answer, but comparison may hold you until the time limit becomes obvious. Manuals, diagrams, photographs, and written feedback give you stable details to inspect and correct. The best explanation can take time needed for a workable choice, especially when pressure makes you even more exact. This is clearest in technical tasks and school feedback; it is a preference, not guaranteed correctness.
bos_sources.takeaway: You naturally seek exact information, checkable details, and a clear result. You can accept a workable answer, but comparison may hold you until the time limit becomes obvious.

bos_sources.headline: Your leverage pattern
bos_sources.text: You combine your own investigation with useful tools, knowledgeable people, and divided work. Help fits best when the question, role, and expected result are clear. You stay close to the problem while gathering missing information and avoiding the delay of doing every part yourself. Vague advice or unclear handoffs may send you back into checking work yourself. Most examples come from repairs, school choices, and technical groups; personal situations may work differently.
bos_sources.takeaway: You combine your own investigation with useful tools, knowledgeable people, and divided work. Help fits best when the question, role, and expected result are clear.

bos_sources.headline: Your adaptability pattern
bos_sources.text: You readily change a method when a test or new information shows it is not working. The purpose usually stays steady, so changing course is not abandoning the goal. You can replace a failed route, revisit a hard section, or stop repetition that is no longer teaching you. Unexplained changes are harder because you cannot see the reason for leaving the original method. This appears across technical work, study, and sport; it does not mean weak commitment or constant novelty.
bos_sources.takeaway: You readily change a method when a test or new information shows it is not working. The purpose usually stays steady, so changing course is not abandoning the goal.

bos_sources.headline: Your structure pattern
bos_sources.text: You like a clear sequence, a definition of finished, and information you can revisit. Plans are useful rails, not fixed rules, and you still want unplanned time. Stable goals and written expectations reduce guessing while leaving room to change the method. Unexplained plans may feel controlling, while too much scheduling can crowd out the open time you need. You lean toward structure without rigidity; your method changes when results change.
bos_sources.takeaway: You like a clear sequence, a definition of finished, and information you can revisit. Plans are useful rails, not fixed rules, and you still want unplanned time.

bos_sources.headline: Your perspective pattern
bos_sources.text: You connect present choices to medium-term life, asking what an option really involves and whether it will still fit later. Your future thinking stays practical rather than fixed. Looking ahead can protect an interest from becoming an obligation and ground choices in real details. Future fit adds comparison, so a deadline may require separating today’s decision from what can remain open. You described a one-year school choice and possible work interests, not a settled long-term plan.
bos_sources.takeaway: You connect present choices to medium-term life, asking what an option really involves and whether it will still fit later. Your future thinking stays practical rather than fixed.

The pressure point is time: several climbing voices and long design comparisons can use the window meant for testing. Your mindset goal links courage to acting with enough understanding, not acting blindly. School is also a goal in its own right, while the two gym sessions, Friday project block, unplanned time, and mostly okay week set the real boundaries.

The coach prefers a reasonable attempt sooner; you want enough explanation to choose what is being tested. The coach is open to discussing a short-talk-then-attempt arrangement, but no length has been agreed, and the reason Thursday expanded remains unknown.

futures.headline: Useful learning continues, but some tests arrive late

futures.first_sign: A session or project block produces plenty of explanation but only a late attempt or an unresolved choice.
futures.details: The current pattern contains progress, not automatic decline: Tuesday’s starting-foot change worked, and written review has helped before. The same precision can also hold attention when several suggestions or options compete. That could limit feedback from the wall and from the design itself, even while motivation stays intact. We do not know whether the blue problem’s main barrier is technical, conversational, emotional, or simply difficult, and we do not yet know the design’s remaining requirements.

futures.headline: Your test-and-revise habit starts carrying more weight
futures.what: By 2026-11-02, the approach already visible on Tuesday becomes more consistent: you use a result to choose the next method. In school, “workable, then improve” begins replacing open-ended comparison.
futures.conditions: You carry one clear question into the next attempt or project decision, and you record enough of the result to avoid restarting the whole explanation.
futures.first_sign: You can name what one attempt ruled in or out, then choose the next test without reopening every option.
futures.details: Changing the starting foot and getting farther is early evidence that action can sharpen your explanation. Your previous route note also shows a usable way to carry learning forward. If that pattern transfers, climbing becomes a series of informative choices, while the design project moves from comparing to building and testing. The remaining uncertainty is consistency: one successful change does not show that every session will protect test time, and a stated school intention is not yet a submitted design.

futures.headline: Clear boundaries give your ideas time to answer back
futures.what: By 2026-11-02, advice and comparison have clear stopping points, so you can run a coach-approved climbing test and make the school design choice while useful time remains.
futures.conditions: You and the coach agree an in-session advice arrangement, and you use the existing Friday block for a workable decision. No extra training or packed schedule is added.
futures.first_sign: The first sign is not finishing the climb; it is an informative attempt and a design decision happening before their windows close.
futures.details: This path relieves the supported obstacle without asking you to lower your standards or obey unexplained advice. A clear test protects judgment; a stopping point protects action. More climbing feedback can clarify the blue overhang, while an earlier workable school choice leaves room to test and improve the project. It still depends on coordination and actual assignment requirements. We do not know what discussion boundary you and the coach would accept, or whether a current design already meets the brief.

futures.headline: You solve blue and build a repeatable test rhythm
futures.what: By 2026-11-02, you solve the blue overhang and can explain the tests that led there. You also submit the workable design choice by September 25 and move into testing it, without turning every free hour into work.
futures.conditions: The climb must remain available with a coach-approved option in existing sessions. You try a reasonable idea before the explanation is perfect, knowing what is being tested; you may pause, ask or decline. The design must meet the actual brief, with school help if needed.
futures.first_sign: You willingly try a reasonable, supervised option while time remains, then use the result to refine—not defend—the next idea.
futures.details: This is bold because it joins your athlete-owned climbing stretch to the school promise of choosing, testing, and improving, without adding ranking or extra load. Confidence would mean acting with enough understanding and resetting from evidence. There is not enough evidence to say the blue is solvable for you within this window: the key technical blocker and route availability are unknown. The useful question is: which move and coach-observed factor currently limit your next safe attempt? Submitting a design also cannot predict a grade.

futures.headline: Comparison keeps taking the time meant for testing
futures.what: By 2026-11-02, the blue problem may remain unfinished or poorly explained because too few ideas reach a useful attempt. A delayed design choice could also squeeze the time available to test and improve it.
futures.conditions: Several voices keep extending climbing discussion, and design comparison continues without a visible workable-for-now line. You keep the existing week, so a lost window is not simply added elsewhere.
futures.first_sign: Another session or Friday block ends with extensive comparison but no informative attempt or workable choice.
futures.details: This is a preventable risk, not a prediction of failure. Thursday already showed how discussion can leave one attempt, and the project has previously come close to a parts-order deadline. If the same time tradeoff repeats, accuracy-seeking blocks the feedback needed for accuracy. Motivation may still be high; the issue is unused test opportunity. We do not know whether upcoming advice will be quieter, whether the current designs are nearly ready, or whether you will notice the time tradeoff earlier.

candidates.action: Ask your coach for one adviser, a brief discussion, then an attempt.
candidates.why: This addresses the exact point where your chosen priority is being lost: several suggestions and long explanation used most of Thursday’s session. It protects your need to understand the test without asking you to train more, and it keeps the coach responsible for deciding which climbing options are appropriate.
candidates.when: Ask before the next Tuesday session begins; if the coach is unavailable, make the same request before Thursday’s existing session.
candidates.who: You ask and decide whether the arrangement works. If agreed, your coach chooses suitable options and supervises while you try one reasonable idea. You may pause, ask a question or decline.
candidates.action_signal: The coach gives a clear yes, no or alternative. If agreed, you know who advises first; then note whether a suitable supervised attempt actually happened.
candidates.progress_signal: If a suitable supervised attempt occurs, check whether you got farther or whether the next blocker seems clearer; separately state whether you understood what was being tested and still had useful session time. If the coach agrees to comment, keep that observation separate; no coach debrief is assumed.
candidates.review: On September 21, you start the check: was an arrangement agreed, did a suitable supervised attempt occur, and what—if anything—did you learn? If no suitable attempt occurred, leave climbing progress untested. You may stop or request a change; the coach may stop for safety or suitability, and any continuation or change remains conditional on both of you agreeing. Preserve school and unplanned time.
candidates.stop_or_change: Change or stop if the coach cannot safely support it, the group setting prevents one-adviser input, you do not want it, or discussion still crowds out attempts.
candidates.bos_fit: You tend to use knowledgeable people well when the question and roles are explicit, while several simultaneous inputs can narrow your speech. An ask-first arrangement gives you choice and a stable frame for experimentation. That fit is supported, but the exact discussion boundary and whether one adviser is practical in this group remain unknown.

Anchoring the choice to the real brief respects precision rather than fighting it. The uncertainty is whether the brief is clear and whether any current option is ready, which is why teacher clarification remains a fallback.

resolution.method: Exact reviewer-prescribed wording applied and independently checked by deterministic equality; no further generation.

issue.problem: The amended language introduces unagreed coach commitments. "Your coach describes what happened on the attempt" assigns the coach a debrief and interpretation role that is neither included in Rowan’s request nor established by the source. "Continue, change or stop together" then presumes coach participation in the September 21 review and can imply that Rowan needs joint agreement to stop, contradicting the adjacent statements that Rowan may decline and that the first step is only an ask. Conditional agreement for the climbing arrangement does not establish either of these later commitments.
issue.source_check: COACH3 supports only the possibility of agreeing a short-discussion-then-normal-attempt arrangement and confirms the coach’s existing responsibility to supervise and choose appropriate options; it does not establish an agreement to describe the result afterward or attend the September 21 review. CONFIRM establishes the review date but not coach participation. A03 and COACH1 document one past result and observation, not an ongoing coach-reporting arrangement. A14-A15 and the amended who/stop language preserve Rowan’s ability to pause, ask, decline, or stop.

If the coach agrees to comment, keep that observation separate; no coach debrief is assumed." Replace review with: "On September 21, you start the check: was an arrangement agreed, did a suitable supervised attempt occur, and what—if anything—did you learn? If no suitable attempt occurred, leave climbing progress untested. You may stop or request a change; the coach may stop for safety or suitability, and any continuation or change remains conditional on both of you agreeing. Preserve school and unplanned time."
